aAbout: Zoom Earth, by Neave Interactive Limited, is an interactive weather map of the world and a real-time hurricane tracker, free on the web, iOS and Android. It shows near real-time satellite imagery — live images from NOAA GOES, JMA Himawari and EUMETSAT Meteosat geostationary satellites updated every 10 minutes, plus HD images updated twice a day from NASA polar-orbiting satellites Aqua and Terra — alongside rain radar with nowcasting, forecast maps from DWD ICON and NOAA GFS, hurricane tracking using NHC, JTWC, NRL and IBTrACS data, and an active fires overlay updated daily with data from NASA FIRMS. No account is required for basic use.
aStrengths: Zoom Earth is the easier live watch: satellite imagery every 10 minutes, rain radar with nowcasting, forecast layers for rain, wind, temperature and pressure, and a dedicated hurricane tracker — presented as a simple consumer weather map on the web and in well-rated mobile apps, free with no account. If your question is 'what is the weather doing right now, and what is this storm about to do?', Zoom Earth answers it in seconds, without a research interface to learn.
bAbout: NASA Worldview is NASA EOSDIS's free, open-source browser for near-real-time satellite imagery: more than 1,000 global, full-resolution layers — fires, storms, air quality, sea ice, vegetation and more — most updated within about three hours of observation, some spanning nearly 30 years, with geostationary imagery in 10-minute increments. It adds event pins for cyclones, wildfires and eruptions, time-lapse animation building, layer comparison (swipe and opacity) and downloadable underlying data via NASA's GIBS services. It is a flat map with polar projections, not a 3D globe, and it is not a weather-forecast product. No signup; it runs in the browser.
bStrengths: NASA Worldview is an extraordinary free research tool: 1,000+ full-resolution satellite layers, most refreshed within about three hours of observation, some spanning nearly 30 years, geostationary imagery in 10-minute increments, event tracking for cyclones, wildfires and eruptions, custom time-lapse animations, layer transparency and comparison tools, and the underlying data downloadable via NASA GIBS — open source, backed by NASA's EOSDIS. For environmental science and disaster analysis, its scientific layer library is unmatched at any price, let alone free.
betterAnswer: They answer different questions. Zoom Earth is better for live weather: what is this storm, rain band or fire doing right now, in a map anyone can read, on web or mobile? NASA Worldview is better for processes and evidence: what is happening across the planet's systems — fires, ice, air quality, vegetation — across 1,000+ science layers, with history and downloadable data. Both are free and need no account; keep Zoom Earth for the daily weather check and Worldview for the deep look.

intro: Zoom Earth and NASA Worldview both show you the planet from space, live and free — and they are built for very different readers. Zoom Earth, by Neave Interactive, is the consumer live-weather satellite: imagery every 10 minutes, rain radar with nowcasting, forecast layers and a hurricane tracker, in an app anyone can read in seconds. NASA Worldview is NASA's science instrument: more than 1,000 near-real-time satellite layers, an archive reaching back nearly 30 years in places, event tracking, time-lapse tools and downloadable data — powerful, and unmistakably a research tool. One is for checking the storm today; the other is for studying the Earth system.
pricingA: Free on the web, iOS and Android, with no account required for basic use. Zoom Earth Pro is listed under In-App Purchases on the official US App Store listing at $1.99 and $11.99 — that listing does not label which billing period each price corresponds to, so the period for each price is unverified. Its terms say subscriptions are billed on a periodic basis (e.g. monthly or annually), as specified at the time of purchase. No free trial for Pro was stated on the official pages checked.
pricingB: Completely free — NASA provides Worldview as a public service through EOSDIS. No paid plans, and no signup is required to browse.

verdictA: Choose Zoom Earth if you want the live weather picture — a storm, a rain band or a fire, on a simple map or in the app, refreshed every 10 minutes — without learning a research tool.
verdictB: Choose NASA Worldview if you want the evidence — 1,000+ science layers, days-to-decades of history, time-lapse and comparison tools and downloadable NASA data for fires, storms, ice and air quality.
verdictLine: Zoom Earth is the daily driver: live weather satellite for everyone, at a glance. NASA Worldview is the laboratory: the deepest free window onto the Earth system ever published. For watching today's storm, open Zoom Earth; for understanding the planet, open Worldview.
worldEye: Zoom Earth and NASA Worldview both stop at the view from space — neither shows you the ground, and neither offers a 3D globe. WorldEye takes the third position: a free 3D globe with 74,229 public cameras across 105 countries alongside live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires, so satellite context and ground-level reality sit in the same view, with a free tier and no signup. Its imagery is neither Zoom Earth's live weather feed nor NASA's science library, and it does not claim to be. Its optional Pro tier is $7.99/week · $13.99/month · $74.99/year.
